title: Yavoriv
summary: Yavoriv is a city located in Lviv Oblast, [[western-ukraine|western Ukraine]], approximately 15 kilometers from the Polish border. It serves as the administrative center of Yavoriv Raion and has a population of approximately 12,785 as of 2022.

sections.heading: Geographical Context
paragraphs: Yavoriv is situated about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) from the Polish border and approximately 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of [[lviv|Lviv]], the capital of [[lviv-oblast|Lviv Oblast]]. The city is the administrative center of Yavoriv Raion and hosts the administration of Yavoriv urban hromada, which is one of the hromadas [[coal-in-ukraine|in Ukraine]].

sections.heading: Historical Significance
paragraphs: The first written mention of Yavoriv dates back to 1436. In 1569, it was granted Magdeburg rights by Polish King Sigismund II Augustus. Yavoriv was a royal town of Poland and a favored residence of King John III Sobieski, who signed the Polish-French Treaty of Jaworów there in 1675. The town was an important commercial center until the [[first-partition-of-poland|First Partition of Poland]] in 1772 when it was annexed by the Habsburg Empire and became part of Austrian [[galicia|Galicia]].

Following World War I, Yavoriv experienced conflict during the Polish-[[full-scale-russo-ukrainian-war|Ukrainian War]]. It became part of the Second Polish Republic until the onset of World War II in September 1939, when it was invaded by Germany. The town was occupied by Soviet forces from 1939 to 1941 and then by German forces until 1944. The Jewish population, which numbered around 3,000 before the German occupation, faced severe persecution during this time.

In 1944, Yavoriv was re-occupied by [[soviet-union|the Soviets]] and was annexed from Poland by the Soviet Union in 1945. The town was a center for sulfur mining from the 1960s to the 1990s, with remnants of this industry still visible today. Yavoriv became part of [[independent-ukraine|independent Ukraine]] following the dissolution of the Soviet Union on 10 December 1991.

sections.heading: Recent Events
paragraphs: On 13 March 2022, during the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Yavoriv was the site of a significant military attack when a Russian missile struck a military base in the city. Russian military officials claimed that the attack resulted in the deaths of up to 180 foreign mercenaries, while [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] sources reported at least 35 fatalities and 134 injuries. The explosion was audible in neighboring Poland.

sections.heading: Notable Figures
paragraphs: Yavoriv has been the birthplace of several notable individuals, including the Russian Orthodox archbishop Stefan Yavorsky (1658–1722), poet Osyp Makovei (1867–1925), and literary historian Ludwik Bernacki (1882–1939). Other notable figures include Vasyl Tuchapets, a bishop of the [[ukrainian-greek-catholic-church|Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church]], General Władysław Langner of the Polish Army, and mathematician Wawrzyniec Żmurko. Rabbi David Altschuler, a prominent Jewish commentator, was also born in Yavoriv and served as rabbi at the local synagogue.
